content: Melting is a physical process in which a substance transitions from a solid state to a liquid state. This occurs when the internal energy of the solid increases, typically through the application of heat, until it reaches a specific temperature known as the melting point. At this temperature, the solid undergoes a phase change and becomes a liquid. Once the substance has completely melted, it is referred to as molten. The melting point is a unique and characteristic property of a substance, but it is not necessarily the same as the freezing point. The difference between melting and freezing points can be observed in phenomena such as supercooling. For example, in the case of water, ice crystals often require a nucleation site, or a seed, to begin forming. On a very clean glass surface, water can remain in a liquid state even when cooled several degrees below its melting point without freezing. In fact, pure water in fine emulsions has been cooled to as low as -38 degrees Celsius without ice nucleation occurring. This highlights why the melting point is considered a defining property of a substance, whereas the freezing point is not. When the internal energy of a substance, such as a gas, is increased by an external energy source, the molecular vibrations within the substance intensify. As these vibrations grow stronger, the substance becomes increasingly ordered. The term fusion is also used to describe the melting process. Melting occurs at a constant temperature, which is the melting point of the substance. Even if additional energy is applied, the temperature does not increase further until the entire substance has transitioned into the liquid phase. From a thermodynamic perspective, at the melting point, the change in Gibbs free energy (ΔG) of the material is zero. This is because both the enthalpy (H) and entropy (S) of the material increase during melting (ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0). The melting process takes place when the Gibbs free energy of the liquid phase becomes lower than that of the solid phase for a given material. The relationship between entropy, enthalpy, and temperature during melting can be expressed as: ΔS = ΔH / T In this equation, T represents the temperature at the melting point, ΔS is the change in entropy during melting, and ΔH is the change in enthalpy during melting. In genetics, the term melting refers to the process of separating double-stranded DNA into two single strands. This can be achieved by applying heat or using specific chemicals. This separation occurs because DNA is composed of two complementary strands that can be denatured under certain conditions.
